# Housing and racial bias {#housing-and-racial-bias .unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.home-lead}
Applied Replication for Data Skills (AR4DS) is a course that introduces technical skills for modern empirical data analysis through an applied 'replication' exercise. This site presents one of its case studies, built around a single published claim, its reanalysis by five independent analysts and its replication with new data.
:::

::: {.home-cta}
[Formats](#formats) [Read the background](background.qmd)
:::

## The course {#the-course .unnumbered}

::: {.home-intro}
The main aim of the course is to introduce technical skills for modern empirical data analysis: finding the data and code of a study in an online repository, working with code so that another person (or your future self) can reproduce your steps, fixing your analytical choices in a preregistration before you run the analysis, and writing a live report that combines code and text.
:::

The claim at the centre of the exercise comes from the work of SCORE, a programme that put claims from published social and behavioural research through reproduction, robustness checks and replication. The exercise follows the design of its robustness study [Multi100\; @AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness] on a smaller scale, with many analysts testing the same claim, each stating their analytical choices, and results reported in a form that allows them to be compared. The AR4DS site describes [the programme](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/score.html), and its page on [the robustness article](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/robustness-article.html) explains how the results of the analysts were placed on one scale and compared.

::::

:::: {.home-rs .home-reveal}

::: {.home-r}
### Reproduction {.unnumbered .unlisted}

Participants choose one of the five independent reanalyses of the claim and repeat it on the public file of the original study, recovering the recorded test statistic and tracing it to the software defaults and coding decisions on which it depends.
:::

::: {.home-r}
### Robustness {.unnumbered .unlisted}

Participants then work through the analytical decisions that lie between the data and a result, trying alternative specifications one change at a time, locating each result on a specification curve of `r h_spec` defensible analyses and – in the day and independent formats – declaring one specification in a short preregistration before it is run.
:::

::: {.home-r}
### Replication {.unnumbered .unlisted}

The course then sets the claim against its replication with new data, a preregistered experiment on 3,050 housing authorities in which no significant gap was found, and in the day and independent formats each participant runs the declared analysis again on the data of that experiment. The course considers what a failed replication can and cannot establish about the original result.
:::

## The case study {#the-case .unnumbered}

::: {.home-intro}
The case study is built around a field experiment published in the *American Journal of Political Science* in 2017, in which the same short email was sent to about a thousand public housing authorities in the United States, each time signed with one of six names meant to indicate a white, a Black or a Hispanic sender. One sentence of its abstract, in the form given to the analysts of the robustness study, became the claim tested in the course:
:::

> "Hispanic housing applicants were ... less likely to be greeted by name than were ... white counterparts" [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect, abstract]

::: {.home-cta}
[Read the background](background.qmd)
:::

::::

:::: {.home-rs .home-reveal}

::: {.home-r}
### Methods {.unnumbered .unlisted}

Proportions and the chi-square test, the linear probability model set against the logit, what conditioning on a reply does to an experiment, randomisation inference and statistical power.
:::

::: {.home-r}
### Data {.unnumbered .unlisted}

Two files shipped with the workspace: the `r format(h_emails, big.mark = ",")` emails of the original experiment, released into the public domain (CC0), and the `r format(h_rep_emails, big.mark = ",")` emails of the SCORE replication, from its de-identified data on the OSF.
:::

## Formats {.unnumbered .home-reveal}

::: {.home-intro .home-reveal}
The facilitator of a course chooses its format, and the link that you receive for a course leads to it. Each card below opens the overview of a format.
:::

:::: {.home-grid}

::: {.home-track .home-reveal}
### [Short](tracks/short/index.qmd) {.unnumbered .unlisted}

[Two halves, in the browser]{.home-meta}

Two halves, with nothing to install and nothing to submit: the claim and the five reanalyses, the estimand statement, the reproduction of one reanalysis by each participant, a look at the menu of analyses and the curve of the claim, and the replication with new data.
:::

::: {.home-track .home-reveal}
### [Day](tracks/day/index.qmd) {.unnumbered .unlisted}

[Four parts, in R on your own machine]{.home-meta}

The claim and the credibility of social science, the estimand and the causal graph, the reproduction of one reanalysis by each participant, the five shared out across the class, and the robustness exercise on which the day centres: the specification menu, the class chart and its submissions, the curve of the claim, one analysis declared before it runs, and its run on the data of the replication.
:::

::: {.home-track .home-reveal}
### [Independent](tracks/independent/index.qmd) {.unnumbered .unlisted}

[Five stages at your own pace, in R]{.home-meta}

The case study for a reader who works alone, in R on your own machine, with the modules of the [companion](companion/index.qmd) between the tasks of the exercise and a project of your own at the end.
:::

## The exercise {.unnumbered .home-reveal}

::: {.home-intro .home-reveal}
Every format works through the same six tasks, or a selection of them. The short format takes the first four and sends nothing to the class chart, while the day and independent formats take all six. The decisions that the tasks ask for fall into three groups: the question that the analysis answers; measurement, how the variables are built; and the model, how it is fitted and its uncertainty judged.
:::

:::: {.home-reveal}

<details>
<summary><span class="home-n">Task 1</span>The setup check</summary>

Check that your tools work before the rest of the work depends on them: the check script of the workspace, or in the short format the setup cell of the deck.

</details>

<details>
<summary><span class="home-n">Task 2</span>The data, the estimand and the graph</summary>

Meet the data of the case study, write the estimand statement behind the claim, and finish the causal graph that goes with it. The graph shows why a comparison of greetings among the replies alone is no longer protected by the random assignment.

</details>

<details>
<summary><span class="home-n">Task 3</span>The reproduction</summary>

Reproduce the value recorded in the robustness study for one of the five analysts, from the public file of the original authors (OAs). The four analysts who recorded a statistic reproduce exactly. One of them, 8PTRZ, recorded $\chi^2$ = `r chi_8ptrz` where the plain test gives `r chi_plain`, and finding out why is part of the task.

</details>

<details>
<summary><span class="home-n">Task 4</span>The menu</summary>

Work through the decisions that lie between the data and a result, try alternatives one change at a time, and send one exploration to the class chart. The [decision map](menu.qmd#map) lays every decision out.

</details>

<details>
<summary><span class="home-n">Task 5</span>Preregistration</summary>

Declare one specification in a short preregistration, run it, report it, and find where it sits among the `r h_spec` specifications of the [curve of the claim](curve.qmd).

</details>

<details>
<summary><span class="home-n">Task 6</span>Replication</summary>

Run the specification that you declared on the data of the SCORE replication, a new experiment of 2020, and place it on the curve of the claim on the new data, beside its place on the curve of the original data.

</details>

::::

The exercise page of each format sets out its tasks, with the tool in which each is done, for the [short](tracks/short/exercise.qmd), [day](tracks/day/exercise.qmd) and [independent](tracks/independent/exercise.qmd) formats.

## Getting started {.unnumbered .home-reveal}

::: {.home-intro .home-reveal}
The short format needs only a browser, because every task of the format is done in its deck, which runs R inside the browser. The day and independent formats do the tasks in the workspace, in your IDE, and install R, an IDE and the workspace as part of their preparation.
:::

:::: {.home-steps .home-reveal}

::: {.home-step}
### R and an IDE {.unnumbered .unlisted}

Install R, Quarto and an IDE (Positron, RStudio, VS Code, etc.), following the steps for your operating system; the short format needs none of them. [Install and check](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/setup.html)
:::

::: {.home-step}
### The workspace {.unnumbered .unlisted}

Download the workspace of the case study as a zip file, open it in your IDE and run the check script. The day and independent formats do their tasks in it. [The workspace](tracks/day/before.qmd#the-workspace)
:::

::: {.home-step}
### The deck {.unnumbered .unlisted}

The decks of the short and day formats run R inside the browser. The short format does every task in its deck, and in the day format the deck shows each step with its output. [Choose a format](#formats)
:::

::: {.home-step}
### The browser lab {.unnumbered .unlisted}

Try the exercise in the browser, without installing anything. With the deck, it is also the fallback when a machine fails on the day. [Open the browser lab](lab.qmd)
:::

## Chris Moreh {.unnumbered}

::: {.home-role}
Lecturer in Sociology, Newcastle University
:::

<!-- The biography is quoted from chrismoreh.com (source: D:/GitHub/chrismoreh-source/index.qmd), as CM asked on 2026-10-25, and copied verbatim from the opening page of the site of the Europeanisation case study. -->

A social scientist interested in the political sociology of migration, mobility, ethnicity and nationalism.

Hailing from Transylvania, trained in anthropology and sociology at [Eötvös Loránd University of Budapest](https://tatk.elte.hu/en/) and [Central European University](https://sociology.ceu.edu/), and with a PhD from [Northumbria University](https://www.northumbria.ac.uk/), I currently work as a Lecturer (Assistant Professor) in Sociology at [Newcastle University (UK)](https://www.ncl.ac.uk/gps/staff/profile/chrismoreh.html).

I approach social research as a comparative, interdisciplinary and multimethodological endeavour. My work has combined ethnographic observation, document analysis, survey methods and statistical modelling.

I'm enthusiastic about transparency and reproducibility in the social sciences, and my [pedagogical approach](https://www.ncl.ac.uk/mediav8/library/file-downloads/research-services/open-research/moreh.pdf) seeks to develop skills that facilitate open and credible research practices.

[chrismoreh.com](https://chrismoreh.com)
